meta.convention: NADH = 2.5 ATP, FADH2 = 1.5 ATP (lecture L.10); 4 H+ = 1 ATP. L.11 glycolysis items that count NADH state their convention in the stem (the slides quote NADH = 3 or 2.5 ATP).

pastPaperSearch.summary: No genuine National University (NU, Oman) or Oman Medical College past-paper MCQs on the TCA cycle, PDH, thiamine or ETC/oxidative phosphorylation were found after about 30 English and Arabic searches covering the open web, Studocu, Quizlet, Scribd, Course Hero, Docsity, SlideShare, Telegram mirrors and Sultan Qaboos University (SQU) queries; no SQU biochemistry papers surfaced either. The only Oman-linked item was an anonymous 2014/15 student upload on Studocu filed under 'Oman Medical College – Biochemistry (MPRC0205)': an essay-style SAQ/LAQ topic list (not MCQs, format typical of generic MBBS question banks, not verifiable as an official OMC/NU paper) whose Biological Oxidation, TCA and Vitamins prompts inspired 8 MCQs here, labelled 'Adapted from OMC-tagged Studocu question bank'. Other documents in that Studocu course were generic (a Sanfoundry-style gluconeogenesis quiz, Lippincott review MCQs). All remaining questions are original, written to the L.10/L.12/L.13 lecture content and Lippincott 9th ed., plus the lecturer's own two MCQs and two open questions. L.11 Glycolysis extension (q126–q175): about 12 further English and Arabic searches plus direct fetches looked specifically for NU/COMHS, Oman Medical College and Sultan Qaboos University (SQU) past-paper MCQs on glycolysis, GLUT/SGLT glucose transporters, hexokinase/glucokinase, pyruvate kinase deficiency, 2,3-BPG and lactic acidosis. None were found. The OMC-tagged Studocu pages listed below now return obfuscated placeholder text to automated fetches, so their contents could not be re-checked and no new item is adapted from them. Everything that surfaced was generic (Brainscape, ditki, Varsity Tutors, Geeky Medics, Lecturio, Wikipedia) or from other universities (e.g., Iraqi lecture files and Telegram channels, a Brainscape deck with no stated institution); none mentioned Oman. All 50 glycolysis questions are therefore original, written to the L.11 slides and Lippincott 9th ed., together with the lecturer's own MCQ on net energy (stem clarified to ask for net substrate-level ATP), a companion item stating the NADH = 3 ATP convention, the lecture case of the 18-year-old with pyruvate kinase deficiency (5 items) and the fluoride-tube question.

questions.stem: In which cellular compartment is the pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex located?
options: Cytosol
Intermembrane space
Outer mitochondrial membrane
Smooth endoplasmic reticulum
Mitochondrial matrix
questions.explanation: The PDH complex is a mitochondrial matrix enzyme, so pyruvate made by cytosolic glycolysis must first be transported into the matrix. The cytosol is the site of glycolysis, not of pyruvate oxidation.

questions.stem: Which equation correctly summarizes the overall reaction catalysed by the PDH complex?
options: Pyruvate + CoA + NAD⁺ → acetyl CoA + CO₂ + NADH + H⁺
Pyruvate + CO₂ + ATP → oxaloacetate + ADP + Pi
Pyruvate + NADH + H⁺ → lactate + NAD⁺
Pyruvate + glutamate → alanine + α-ketoglutarate
Pyruvate + CoA + FAD → acetyl CoA + CO₂ + FADH₂
questions.explanation: PDH oxidatively decarboxylates pyruvate (3C) to acetyl CoA (2C), releasing CO₂ and reducing NAD⁺ to NADH. FAD is a bound carrier on E3 that is re-oxidized by NAD⁺, so the net reduced product is NADH, not FADH₂; the other equations are the pyruvate carboxylase, LDH and ALT reactions.

questions.stem: The conversion of pyruvate to acetyl CoA by the PDH complex is best classified as:
options: Substrate-level phosphorylation
Carboxylation
Oxidative decarboxylation
Transamination
Hydration
questions.explanation: Pyruvate loses one carbon as CO₂ (decarboxylation) while the remaining two-carbon unit is oxidized, with the electrons passed to NAD⁺. Carboxylation (adding CO₂) is the pyruvate carboxylase reaction, the opposite process.

questions.stem: The five coenzymes of the PDH complex are remembered by the mnemonic “Tender Loving Care For Nobody”. Which list is correct?
options: TPP, biotin, CoA, FAD, NAD⁺
TPP, lipoic acid, CoA, FAD, NAD⁺
PLP, lipoic acid, CoA, FMN, NADP⁺
TPP, lipoic acid, biotin, FMN, NAD⁺
THF, lipoic acid, CoA, FAD, NADP⁺
questions.explanation: Tender = thiamine pyrophosphate, Loving = lipoic acid, Care = coenzyme A, For = FAD, Nobody = NAD⁺. Biotin belongs to carboxylases such as pyruvate carboxylase, not to PDH.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with severe malnutrition has combined deficiencies of thiamine, riboflavin, niacin and pantothenic acid. Which coenzyme of his PDH complex would NOT be directly affected by these vitamin deficiencies?
options: Lipoic acid
Thiamine pyrophosphate
FAD
NAD⁺
Coenzyme A
questions.explanation: Lipoic acid is synthesized in the body and is not derived from a B vitamin. TPP comes from thiamine (B1), FAD from riboflavin (B2), NAD⁺ from niacin (B3) and CoA from pantothenic acid (B5).

questions.stem: Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) is the coenzyme of which component of the PDH complex?
options: E2 – dihydrolipoyl transacetylase
E3 – dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase
E1 – pyruvate decarboxylase
PDH kinase
PDH phosphatase
questions.explanation: E1 (pyruvate decarboxylase) uses TPP to decarboxylate pyruvate. E2 uses lipoic acid and CoA to form acetyl CoA, and E3 uses FAD and NAD⁺ to regenerate oxidized lipoamide.

questions.stem: Which pair of coenzymes is used by E3 (dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase) of the PDH complex?
options: TPP and lipoic acid
Lipoic acid and CoA
TPP and CoA
FAD and NAD⁺
Biotin and NAD⁺
questions.explanation: E3 re-oxidizes the reduced lipoamide of E2: electrons pass to FAD and then to NAD⁺, producing NADH. Lipoic acid and CoA are the coenzymes of E2 (transacetylase).

questions.stem: Pantothenic acid (vitamin B5) is a component of coenzyme A. Which step of the PDH reaction directly depends on this coenzyme?
options: Decarboxylation of pyruvate by E1
Re-oxidation of reduced lipoamide by FAD on E3
Transfer of the acetyl group from the lipoamide arm of E2 to form acetyl CoA
Transfer of electrons from FADH₂ to NAD⁺ on E3
Phosphorylation of E1 by PDH kinase
questions.explanation: E2 (dihydrolipoyl transacetylase) transfers the acetyl group from its lipoamide arm to CoA, forming acetyl CoA. Decarboxylation uses TPP on E1, and FAD and NAD⁺ act on E3.

questions.stem: A patient with angular cheilitis and glossitis is diagnosed with riboflavin (vitamin B2) deficiency. Which component of the PDH complex is most directly compromised?
options: E1 – pyruvate decarboxylase, which needs TPP
E2 – transacetylase, which needs coenzyme A
PDH kinase, which needs ATP
PDH phosphatase, which needs Ca²⁺
E3 – dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase, which needs FAD
questions.explanation: Riboflavin is the precursor of FAD, the coenzyme of E3 that re-oxidizes lipoamide and passes the electrons to NAD⁺. TPP (E1) is thiamine-derived and CoA (E2) is pantothenate-derived.

questions.stem: In which of the following cells would the PDH complex be ABSENT?
options: Neurons
Cardiac muscle cells
Renal tubular cells
Hepatocytes
Mature red blood cells
questions.explanation: PDH is present in all tissues that contain mitochondria, especially kidney, brain and heart. Mature erythrocytes have no mitochondria, so they cannot oxidize pyruvate and convert it to lactate instead.

questions.stem: The PDH reaction is physiologically irreversible. Which metabolic consequence follows directly from this?
options: Pyruvate can be regenerated from acetyl CoA only in the liver
Lactate can no longer be used for gluconeogenesis
Acetyl CoA cannot be converted back to pyruvate, so it cannot be used for net glucose synthesis
Alanine cannot be transaminated to pyruvate
Fatty acids become the main substrate for gluconeogenesis
questions.explanation: Because PDH is irreversible, carbon that reaches acetyl CoA cannot return to pyruvate and on to glucose. Lactate and alanine remain gluconeogenic because they are converted to pyruvate before the PDH step.

questions.stem: In the well-fed state, high mitochondrial ATP, acetyl CoA and NADH activate PDH kinase. What happens to the PDH complex?
options: E1 is phosphorylated and the complex is activated
E1 is dephosphorylated and the complex is activated
The complex is converted into pyruvate carboxylase
E1 is phosphorylated and the complex is inactivated
The complex is exported from the matrix to the cytosol
questions.explanation: PDH kinase phosphorylates E1 and switches the complex off, sparing pyruvate when energy and acetyl CoA are abundant; PDH phosphatase reverses this. This covalent control is a feature of PDH that the α-KGDH complex does not share.

questions.stem: Which condition would INCREASE the activity of the PDH complex?
options: A high mitochondrial NADH/NAD⁺ ratio
A high acetyl CoA/CoA ratio
A high ATP/ADP ratio
Increased activity of PDH kinase
A rise in mitochondrial Ca²⁺ during muscle contraction, which activates PDH phosphatase
questions.explanation: Ca²⁺ stimulates PDH phosphatase, which dephosphorylates and activates E1, matching pyruvate oxidation to muscle work. High NADH, acetyl CoA and ATP signal abundant energy, activate PDH kinase and therefore inactivate the complex.

questions.stem: The PDH complex is found in all mitochondria-containing tissues. In which group of tissues is it particularly important, as taught?
options: Erythrocytes, lens and cornea
Adipose tissue, bone and cartilage
Skin, hair follicles and nails
Kidney, brain and heart
Lymph nodes and spleen only
questions.explanation: The lecture highlights kidney, brain and heart, which rely heavily on aerobic oxidation of pyruvate. Erythrocytes lack mitochondria entirely and depend on anaerobic glycolysis.

questions.stem: Which enzyme complex of the TCA cycle has the same three-enzyme architecture (E1, E2, E3) and the same five coenzymes as the PDH complex?
options: Isocitrate dehydrogenase
Succinate dehydrogenase
Citrate synthase
Malate dehydrogenase
α-Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex
questions.explanation: α-KGDH is a PDH-like multienzyme complex (E1, E2, E3) using TPP, lipoic acid, CoA, FAD and NAD⁺. Isocitrate dehydrogenase also performs an oxidative decarboxylation but is a single enzyme.

questions.stem: Isocitrate dehydrogenase, the PDH complex and the α-KGDH complex all catalyse oxidative decarboxylations. How does isocitrate dehydrogenase differ from the other two?
options: It is a three-enzyme complex with E1, E2 and E3 components
It is a single enzyme that uses NAD⁺ (or NADP⁺) and does not need TPP or lipoic acid
It requires thiamine pyrophosphate as its coenzyme
It does not release CO₂
It uses FAD as its final electron acceptor
questions.explanation: As taught, isocitrate dehydrogenase is a single enzyme using NAD⁺/NADP⁺, whereas PDH, α-KGDH and branched-chain α-keto acid DH are E1–E2–E3 complexes with five coenzymes. It still releases CO₂ (isocitrate 6C → α-ketoglutarate 5C).

questions.stem: The branched-chain α-keto acid dehydrogenase complex functions mainly in:
options: Conversion of α-ketoglutarate to succinyl CoA in the TCA cycle
Catabolism of the branched-chain amino acids leucine, isoleucine and valine
Glycolysis in the cytosol
Fatty acid synthesis
The urea cycle
questions.explanation: It oxidatively decarboxylates the α-keto acids derived from leucine, isoleucine and valine, using the same E1–E2–E3 design and five coenzymes as PDH. Conversion of α-ketoglutarate to succinyl CoA is the job of α-KGDH.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman with prolonged poor oral intake after bariatric surgery is found to be thiamine-deficient. Which set of enzyme complexes would show reduced activity?
options: Isocitrate DH, malate DH and citrate synthase
Succinate DH, fumarase and aconitase
PDH complex only
Pyruvate carboxylase, ALT and AST
PDH complex, α-KGDH complex and branched-chain α-keto acid DH complex
questions.explanation: All three α-keto acid dehydrogenase complexes use TPP on their E1 component, so all are impaired in thiamine deficiency. Isocitrate DH, malate DH and the other listed enzymes do not use TPP.

questions.stem: Which pair of products is common to the reactions catalysed by the PDH complex and the α-KGDH complex?
options: CO₂ and NADH
GTP and FADH₂
Citrate and CoA
ATP and H₂O
Oxaloacetate and NADH
questions.explanation: Both are oxidative decarboxylations: each releases one CO₂ and reduces NAD⁺ to NADH, and each forms a CoA thioester (acetyl CoA or succinyl CoA). GTP is made in the next TCA step by succinyl CoA synthetase.

questions.stem: The α-KGDH complex, the TCA-cycle analogue of PDH, converts α-ketoglutarate into:
options: Succinate + GTP
Glutamate + NAD⁺
Succinyl CoA + CO₂ + NADH
Fumarate + FADH₂
Oxaloacetate + NADH
questions.explanation: α-Ketoglutarate (5C) is oxidatively decarboxylated to the 4C thioester succinyl CoA, releasing CO₂ and NADH, exactly as pyruvate is converted to acetyl CoA. Succinate + GTP is formed in the following step by succinate thiokinase.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares the regulation of the PDH complex with that of the α-KGDH complex?
options: PDH is regulated by phosphorylation (PDH kinase/phosphatase), whereas α-KGDH is not; both are inhibited by NADH
Both complexes are switched off by phosphorylation by specific kinases
α-KGDH is activated by succinyl CoA, whereas PDH is activated by acetyl CoA
Neither complex is affected by the NADH/NAD⁺ ratio
α-KGDH is inhibited by Ca²⁺, whereas PDH phosphatase is activated by Ca²⁺
questions.explanation: PDH is controlled by covalent modification (kinase inactivates, phosphatase activates), whereas α-KGDH is controlled allosterically: inhibited by NADH and succinyl CoA (and ATP, as taught) and activated by Ca²⁺. Ca²⁺ therefore stimulates both complexes.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department with progressive lethargy, poor feeding and rapid breathing. Examination shows generalized hypotonia and severe developmental delay. Plasma lactate is elevated and plasma alanine is markedly elevated. Which enzyme is most likely impaired?
options: Citrate synthase
Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex
α-Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex
Isocitrate dehydrogenase
Malate dehydrogenase
questions.explanation: A block at PDH traps pyruvate, which is diverted to lactate (LDH) and alanine (ALT), causing congenital lactic acidosis with neurological signs. The markedly raised alanine points to pyruvate accumulation, i.e., a block before the cycle rather than at a TCA enzyme.

questions.stem: In an infant with PDH deficiency, why is plasma alanine elevated?
options: Muscle protein is broken down because of hypotonia
Excess acetyl CoA is converted to alanine
Lactate is directly aminated to alanine by LDH
Accumulated pyruvate is transaminated to alanine by alanine transaminase (ALT)
Glutamate dehydrogenase converts pyruvate to alanine
questions.explanation: With PDH blocked, pyruvate accumulates and is converted to lactate (LDH) and to alanine (ALT). Acetyl CoA from pyruvate is decreased, not increased, in PDH deficiency.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old with seizures and poor coordination is suspected of having congenital PDH deficiency. Which blood profile best supports this diagnosis?
options: ↓ Pyruvate, ↓ lactate, ↑ alanine
↑ Pyruvate, ↓ lactate, ↓ alanine
↑ Pyruvate, ↑ lactate, ↑ alanine
Normal lactate with ↑ ammonia
↑ Ketone bodies with ↓ lactate
questions.explanation: PDH deficiency causes accumulation of pyruvate and of its two alternative products, lactate and alanine. This is why it is a major cause of congenital lactic acidosis.

questions.stem: A child with PDH deficiency has hypotonia, developmental delay and seizures. Why does this enzyme defect predominantly damage the nervous system?
options: Neurons lack mitochondria
The brain uses fatty acids as its main fuel
Acetyl CoA accumulates and is directly neurotoxic
PDH is not normally present in the brain
The brain depends heavily on aerobic oxidation of glucose-derived pyruvate for its ATP
questions.explanation: The brain relies on glucose oxidation via PDH and the TCA cycle, so blocking pyruvate entry causes energy failure in neurons. The brain is one of the tissues with especially high PDH activity, and acetyl CoA from pyruvate falls rather than accumulates.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old girl has tachypnoea, hypotonia and a markedly raised blood lactate. Enzyme studies in cultured fibroblasts show low PDH complex activity. Her condition is best classified as:
options: Congenital lactic acidosis due to impaired pyruvate oxidation
Hyperammonaemia due to a urea cycle defect
Haemolytic anaemia due to a glycolytic enzyme defect
Phenylketonuria due to a phenylalanine hydroxylase defect
Diabetic ketoacidosis due to insulin deficiency
questions.explanation: PDH deficiency is a major cause of congenital lactic acidosis in infants and young children: pyruvate that cannot be converted to acetyl CoA is reduced to lactate. The other conditions involve different enzymes and different metabolites.

questions.stem: An infant with confirmed PDH deficiency has persistent lactic acidosis. Which dietary approach most logically reduces lactate production?
options: A low-carbohydrate, high-fat (ketogenic) diet
A high-carbohydrate diet with frequent glucose feeds
Continuous intravenous glucose infusion
A high-protein diet rich in alanine
A lactate-enriched infant formula
questions.explanation: Restricting carbohydrate reduces pyruvate formation, while fat-derived acetyl CoA and ketone bodies supply the TCA cycle without passing through PDH. Extra glucose or alanine would increase pyruvate and worsen the lactic acidosis.

questions.stem: A malnourished chronic alcoholic is brought in confused and hypoglycaemic. Why must thiamine be given immediately, either right before or together with intravenous glucose?
options: Thiamine is required for glucose absorption from the intestine
Thiamine is the coenzyme of hexokinase, so glucose cannot be phosphorylated without it
Glucose increases flux to pyruvate and through TPP-dependent PDH and α-KGDH; without thiamine this worsens lactic acidosis and can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy
Glucose destroys thiamine in plasma, so thiamine must be given first to protect it
Thiamine stimulates insulin secretion and prevents rebound hypoglycaemia
questions.explanation: A glucose load raises glycolytic production of pyruvate, which needs TPP-dependent PDH (and then α-KGDH) to be oxidized; in thiamine depletion the pyruvate is shunted to lactate and the brain's energy supply fails. Hexokinase does not need TPP, and intravenous glucose bypasses intestinal absorption.
questions.origin: Adapted from Lecture L.12 critical-thinking question (options written for this bank)

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with long-standing alcohol misuse presents with confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia. Deficiency of which coenzyme is most responsible?
options: Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP)
Flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD)
Biotin
Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP)
Coenzyme A
questions.explanation: This is Wernicke encephalopathy (part of Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome), caused by thiamine deficiency that cripples the TPP-dependent PDH and α-KGDH complexes in the brain. Alcoholics are at risk because of poor intake and impaired absorption.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man whose diet consists mainly of polished white rice presents with peripheral oedema, breathlessness, tachycardia and cardiomegaly. Echocardiography shows a high-output state. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Pellagra due to niacin deficiency
Scurvy due to vitamin C deficiency
Megaloblastic anaemia due to folate deficiency
Wet beriberi due to thiamine deficiency
Osteomalacia due to vitamin D deficiency
questions.explanation: Wet beriberi is the cardiac form of thiamine deficiency: impaired PDH and α-KGDH cause energy failure in the heart, leading to high-output congestive heart failure. Pellagra instead presents with dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia.
questions.origin: Adapted from OMC-tagged Studocu question bank (essay prompt converted to MCQ; unverified student upload)

questions.stem: A malnourished patient with thiamine deficiency has both heart failure and encephalopathy. Why are the heart and brain affected most?
options: They have the highest aerobic metabolic demand and depend on TPP-dependent PDH and α-KGDH for ATP
They are the only tissues that store thiamine
They lack the enzyme lactate dehydrogenase
They obtain their ATP mainly from anaerobic glycolysis
They use thiamine as a structural protein
questions.explanation: Thiamine deficiency impairs PDH and α-KGDH, causing an energy failure that selectively damages the tissues with the highest metabolic and glucose demands: the heart (wet beriberi) and the brain (Wernicke–Korsakoff). Tissues relying on anaerobic glycolysis would be spared, not targeted.

questions.stem: In a patient with severe thiamine deficiency, which metabolites are expected to accumulate in blood?
options: Acetyl CoA and citrate
Pyruvate, lactate and α-ketoglutarate
Succinyl CoA and fumarate
Oxaloacetate and malate
Ammonia and glutamine
questions.explanation: Without TPP, PDH and α-KGDH cannot act on their α-keto acid substrates, so pyruvate (with lactate derived from it) and α-ketoglutarate build up. The products downstream of these blocks, such as acetyl CoA and succinyl CoA, decrease.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with chronic alcoholism and poor nutrition is found unconscious; his blood glucose is 2.2 mmol/L. Which initial management is most appropriate?
options: Intravenous dextrose alone; thiamine is unnecessary
Intravenous dextrose now and oral thiamine after he recovers
Intravenous insulin with dextrose
Intravenous thiamine immediately before or together with intravenous dextrose
Intravenous bicarbonate before any glucose
questions.explanation: In alcoholics and malnourished patients thiamine must be given immediately, concurrently with or just before glucose, so that the extra pyruvate from glucose can be oxidized by TPP-dependent PDH. Delaying thiamine risks precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy and lactic acidosis.

questions.stem: In a thiamine-deficient patient, ATP production by the heart falls mainly because:
options: Complex IV can no longer transfer electrons to O₂
Pyruvate cannot enter the TCA cycle as acetyl CoA, and α-KGDH flux within the cycle is reduced
The Fo channel of ATP synthase is blocked
Pyruvate kinase can no longer perform substrate-level phosphorylation
Glucose can no longer enter cardiac cells
questions.explanation: TPP is needed by PDH and α-KGDH, so fewer NADH and FADH₂ are delivered to the ETC and ATP synthesis falls. The ETC complexes and ATP synthase themselves are intact; the shortage is of reduced coenzymes.

questions.stem: Which of these patients is at greatest risk of developing Wernicke encephalopathy if given intravenous glucose without thiamine?
options: A well-nourished 25-year-old athlete after a marathon
A patient on long-term isoniazid therapy with a normal diet
A 50-year-old man with chronic alcoholism and a poor diet
A healthy adult who eats raw egg white daily
An exclusively breast-fed infant of a well-nourished mother
questions.explanation: Chronic alcoholics combine poor thiamine intake with impaired absorption and storage, so a glucose load can exhaust the remaining TPP and precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy. Isoniazid causes B6 deficiency and raw egg white (avidin) causes biotin deficiency.

questions.stem: In a chronic alcoholic with severe thiamine deficiency, which TCA-cycle enzyme loses activity in addition to the PDH complex?
options: α-Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex
Isocitrate dehydrogenase
Succinate thiokinase
Malate dehydrogenase
Fumarase
questions.explanation: α-KGDH is a PDH-like complex whose E1 uses TPP, which is why thiamine deficiency impairs the TCA cycle itself and not only the entry of pyruvate. Isocitrate dehydrogenase uses NAD⁺/NADP⁺ only.

questions.stem: Which enzyme catalyses the condensation of acetyl CoA with oxaloacetate to form citrate?
options: Aconitase
Isocitrate dehydrogenase
Malate dehydrogenase
Pyruvate carboxylase
Citrate synthase
questions.explanation: Citrate synthase joins acetyl CoA (2C) and oxaloacetate (4C) to form citrate (6C) in a condensation reaction. Pyruvate carboxylase makes oxaloacetate from pyruvate but does not form citrate.

questions.stem: The conversion of citrate to isocitrate by aconitase is an example of which reaction type?
options: Oxidative decarboxylation
Condensation
Substrate-level phosphorylation
Dehydrogenation
Isomerization
questions.explanation: Aconitase rearranges citrate into its isomer isocitrate; both have six carbons and no carbon or electrons are removed. The first oxidative decarboxylation occurs in the next step, at isocitrate dehydrogenase.

questions.stem: Which reaction of the TCA cycle converts a six-carbon compound into a five-carbon compound?
options: Citrate → isocitrate
α-Ketoglutarate → succinyl CoA
Succinate → fumarate
Isocitrate → α-ketoglutarate
Malate → oxaloacetate
questions.explanation: Isocitrate dehydrogenase removes one carbon as CO₂, turning isocitrate (6C) into α-ketoglutarate (5C) and producing NADH. α-Ketoglutarate → succinyl CoA is the 5C → 4C step.

questions.stem: The two CO₂ molecules released in each turn of the TCA cycle are produced by which enzymes?
options: Isocitrate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex
Citrate synthase and aconitase
Succinate dehydrogenase and fumarase
PDH complex and isocitrate dehydrogenase
α-Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex and malate dehydrogenase
questions.explanation: The two oxidative decarboxylations of the cycle occur at isocitrate DH (6C → 5C) and α-KGDH (5C → 4C). PDH also releases CO₂, but it is the link reaction before the cycle, not part of it.

questions.stem: Which TCA-cycle enzyme generates GTP by substrate-level phosphorylation?
options: α-Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex
Succinate dehydrogenase
Malate dehydrogenase
Citrate synthase
Succinate thiokinase (succinyl CoA synthetase)
questions.explanation: Succinyl CoA synthetase uses the energy of the succinyl CoA thioester bond to make GTP from GDP + Pi, the only substrate-level phosphorylation in the cycle. Succinate dehydrogenase, the next enzyme, produces FADH₂.

questions.stem: Which TCA-cycle enzyme uses FAD and also functions as Complex II of the electron transport chain?
options: Malate dehydrogenase
Isocitrate dehydrogenase
α-Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex
Fumarase
Succinate dehydrogenase
questions.explanation: Succinate dehydrogenase oxidizes succinate to fumarate, reducing FAD to FADH₂, and passes the electrons to coenzyme Q as Complex II. The other dehydrogenases of the cycle reduce NAD⁺.

questions.stem: Fumarase converts fumarate to malate. Which reaction type is this?
options: Dehydrogenation
Isomerization
Decarboxylation
Hydration
Condensation
questions.explanation: Fumarase adds water across the double bond of fumarate to form malate; both are four-carbon compounds. No electrons are removed, so no NADH or FADH₂ is formed in this step.

questions.stem: Malate dehydrogenase catalyses the final step of the TCA cycle. What are its products?
options: Oxaloacetate + FADH₂
Fumarate + H₂O
Citrate + CoA
Oxaloacetate + NADH + H⁺
Succinate + GTP
questions.explanation: Malate is oxidized to oxaloacetate with reduction of NAD⁺ to NADH, regenerating the four-carbon acceptor for the next acetyl CoA. FADH₂ is produced only at the succinate dehydrogenase step.

questions.stem: If the mitochondrial NAD⁺ pool became almost completely reduced to NADH (for example, when the ETC is blocked), which three TCA-cycle enzymes would be directly deprived of their coenzyme?
options: Citrate synthase, aconitase and fumarase
Succinate dehydrogenase, fumarase and malate dehydrogenase
Isocitrate dehydrogenase, succinate dehydrogenase and succinate thiokinase
α-Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex, succinate dehydrogenase and citrate synthase
Isocitrate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex and malate dehydrogenase
questions.explanation: Steps 3, 4 and 8 (isocitrate DH, α-KGDH and malate DH) use NAD⁺ as electron acceptor and produce the 3 NADH of each turn. Succinate dehydrogenase uses FAD, and citrate synthase, aconitase and fumarase do not use NAD⁺.

questions.stem: Which sequence lists the TCA-cycle intermediates in the order in which they are formed?
options: Citrate → α-ketoglutarate → isocitrate → succinyl CoA → succinate → fumarate → malate → oxaloacetate
Citrate → isocitrate → α-ketoglutarate → succinate → succinyl CoA → fumarate → malate → oxaloacetate
Citrate → isocitrate → α-ketoglutarate → succinyl CoA → succinate → fumarate → malate → oxaloacetate
Citrate → isocitrate → α-ketoglutarate → succinyl CoA → succinate → malate → fumarate → oxaloacetate
Citrate → isocitrate → succinyl CoA → α-ketoglutarate → succinate → fumarate → malate → oxaloacetate
questions.explanation: Starting from citrate, the cycle passes through isocitrate, α-ketoglutarate, succinyl CoA, succinate, fumarate and malate before regenerating oxaloacetate. Succinyl CoA always precedes succinate, and fumarate precedes malate.

questions.stem: Which TCA-cycle enzyme is NOT a soluble enzyme of the mitochondrial matrix?
options: Succinate dehydrogenase
Citrate synthase
Fumarase
Malate dehydrogenase
Isocitrate dehydrogenase
questions.explanation: Succinate dehydrogenase is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane because it is also Complex II of the ETC. The other TCA enzymes are soluble matrix enzymes.

questions.stem: Acetyl CoA (2C) combines with oxaloacetate (4C) to form citrate (6C). By the end of one complete turn of the cycle, what has happened to the carbon balance?
options: Three CO₂ have been released and pyruvate has been regenerated
No CO₂ has been released; the carbons are stored as succinate
One CO₂ has been released and citrate has been regenerated
Both acetyl carbons have been converted into glucose
Two carbons have been released as CO₂ and oxaloacetate (4C) has been regenerated
questions.explanation: Two decarboxylations (isocitrate DH and α-KGDH) release two CO₂ per turn, balancing the two carbons that entered, so oxaloacetate is regenerated with no net gain or loss of intermediates.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the TCA cycle?
options: It occurs in the mitochondrial matrix and is the common final pathway for oxidation of carbohydrates, fats and amino acids
It occurs in the cytosol and oxidizes glucose anaerobically
It occurs in the inner mitochondrial membrane and makes most ATP directly from a proton gradient
It occurs in the endoplasmic reticulum and detoxifies drugs
It operates only during fasting, to convert acetyl CoA into glucose
questions.explanation: The TCA cycle is the second stage of aerobic respiration; it runs in the matrix and oxidizes acetyl CoA from all fuels to CO₂. Most ATP is made afterwards by oxidative phosphorylation, not by the cycle itself.

questions.stem: In a patient with severe hypoxaemia, TCA-cycle activity in the brain falls even though no TCA reaction uses O₂ directly. Why?
options: Citrate synthase uses O₂ as a co-substrate
Aconitase contains a heme group that must bind O₂
CO₂ cannot be released in the absence of O₂
NAD⁺ and FAD can only be regenerated from NADH and FADH₂ by the O₂-dependent electron transport chain
GTP synthesis by succinate thiokinase requires O₂
questions.explanation: The cycle's dehydrogenases need a continuous supply of oxidized NAD⁺ and FAD, which is provided only when the ETC passes electrons to O₂. Without O₂, NADH and FADH₂ accumulate and the dehydrogenase steps halt.

questions.stem: When succinyl CoA is converted to succinate, the energy used to form GTP comes from:
options: The proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane
Cleavage of the high-energy thioester bond of succinyl CoA
Oxidation of FADH₂ by Complex II
Hydrolysis of ATP
Decarboxylation of succinyl CoA
questions.explanation: This is substrate-level phosphorylation: the free energy of the thioester bond is used directly to phosphorylate GDP. The proton gradient drives ATP synthase in oxidative phosphorylation, a different mechanism.

questions.stem: Which pair of TCA-cycle intermediates both contain six carbon atoms?
options: Isocitrate and α-ketoglutarate
α-Ketoglutarate and succinyl CoA
Citrate and isocitrate
Succinate and fumarate
Oxaloacetate and citrate
questions.explanation: Citrate and isocitrate are both 6C (aconitase only isomerizes). α-Ketoglutarate is 5C, while succinyl CoA, succinate, fumarate, malate and oxaloacetate are 4C.

questions.stem: Oxidation of one acetyl CoA in the TCA cycle produces:
options: 2 NADH, 2 FADH₂, 1 GTP and 2 CO₂
3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP and 2 CO₂
3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 2 GTP and 3 CO₂
4 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP and 2 CO₂
3 NADH, 2 FADH₂, 1 GTP and 1 CO₂
questions.explanation: NADH comes from isocitrate DH, α-KGDH and malate DH; FADH₂ from succinate DH; GTP from succinate thiokinase; and the two CO₂ from the two oxidative decarboxylations. A fourth NADH and third CO₂ belong to the PDH step, which precedes the cycle.

questions.stem: Using the convention NADH = 2.5 ATP and FADH₂ = 1.5 ATP, how many ATP are obtained from complete oxidation of one acetyl CoA through the TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation?
options: 7.5 ATP
8.5 ATP
9 ATP
10 ATP
12 ATP
questions.explanation: 3 NADH × 2.5 = 7.5, plus 1 FADH₂ × 1.5 = 1.5, plus 1 GTP = 1, giving 10 ATP. The value 12 comes from the older convention (NADH = 3, FADH₂ = 2).

questions.stem: Using NADH = 2.5 ATP and FADH₂ = 1.5 ATP, approximately how many ATP are produced when one pyruvate is completely oxidized to CO₂ and H₂O in the mitochondria?
options: 10 ATP
12.5 ATP
15 ATP
20 ATP
25 ATP
questions.explanation: The PDH step gives 1 NADH (2.5 ATP) and the TCA cycle gives 10 ATP per acetyl CoA, so 12.5 ATP per pyruvate. The value 15 would result from the older convention (3 + 12).

questions.stem: What is the total ATP yield from the complete aerobic oxidation of one glucose molecule? Use NADH = 2.5 ATP and FADH₂ = 1.5 ATP, and assume cytosolic NADH enters the mitochondria via the malate–aspartate shuttle.
options: 2 ATP
4 ATP
12.5 ATP
25 ATP
32 ATP
questions.explanation: Glycolysis gives 2 ATP + 2 NADH (5 ATP), PDH gives 2 NADH (5 ATP) and the TCA cycle gives 2 × 10 = 20 ATP, a total of about 32 ATP. With the older convention (NADH = 3, FADH₂ = 2) the same calculation gives 38.
questions.origin: Adapted from Lecture L.13 critical-thinking question (options written for this bank)

questions.stem: If the two cytosolic NADH from glycolysis enter the mitochondria via the glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle (delivering their electrons as FADH₂), what is the approximate ATP yield per glucose (NADH = 2.5, FADH₂ = 1.5)?
options: 2 ATP
12.5 ATP
20 ATP
30 ATP
38 ATP
questions.explanation: Each cytosolic NADH is now worth 1.5 instead of 2.5 ATP, so the total falls from 32 (malate–aspartate shuttle) to 30. The value 38 is the older-convention maximum and 20 is the TCA-cycle contribution alone.
questions.origin: Adapted from OMC-tagged Studocu question bank (essay prompt converted to MCQ; unverified student upload)

questions.stem: Using the OLDER Lippincott convention mentioned on the slides (NADH = 3 ATP, FADH₂ = 2 ATP), how many ATP are produced per acetyl CoA oxidized in the TCA cycle?
options: 12 ATP
15 ATP
18 ATP
24 ATP
36 ATP
questions.explanation: 3 NADH × 3 = 9, plus 1 FADH₂ × 2 = 2, plus 1 GTP = 12 ATP under the older convention. The current convention used in this course gives 10.

questions.stem: How many ATP are generated when one molecule of succinate is oxidized to oxaloacetate in the TCA cycle (NADH = 2.5, FADH₂ = 1.5)?
options: 1.5 ATP
2.5 ATP
4 ATP
5 ATP
6 ATP
questions.explanation: Succinate → fumarate gives 1 FADH₂ (1.5 ATP), fumarate → malate gives none, and malate → oxaloacetate gives 1 NADH (2.5 ATP): 4 ATP in total. The value 5 results from wrongly applying the older convention.

questions.stem: How many ATP are generated when one α-ketoglutarate is converted to oxaloacetate through the TCA cycle (NADH = 2.5, FADH₂ = 1.5, GTP = 1 ATP)?
options: 4 ATP
5 ATP
6.5 ATP
7.5 ATP
10 ATP
questions.explanation: α-KGDH gives NADH (2.5), succinate thiokinase gives GTP (1), succinate DH gives FADH₂ (1.5) and malate DH gives NADH (2.5): 7.5 ATP in total. Forgetting the GTP gives 6.5.

questions.stem: In a patient in circulatory shock, severely hypoxic tissues cannot use the TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation, and glucose is metabolized only to lactate. What is the net ATP yield per glucose under these conditions?
options: 0 ATP
2 ATP
4 ATP
12.5 ATP
30 ATP
questions.explanation: Anaerobic glycolysis yields a net 2 ATP per glucose by substrate-level phosphorylation, compared with about 32 when the TCA cycle and ETC operate. Four ATP are formed in total, but 2 are consumed in the early steps.

questions.stem: The citric acid cycle is regulated at three distinct points. One of the regulatory enzymes is isocitrate dehydrogenase. Which of the following are inhibitors of this enzyme?
options: NADH and ATP
Calcium and NADH
ATP and citrate
Succinyl CoA and NADH
ADP and NADH
questions.explanation: Isocitrate dehydrogenase is inhibited by NADH and ATP (signals of high energy) and activated by Ca²⁺ and ADP. Succinyl CoA inhibits citrate synthase and α-KGDH, not isocitrate dehydrogenase.

questions.stem: Which three enzymes are the regulated control points of the TCA cycle, as taught?
options: Aconitase, fumarase and malate dehydrogenase
Succinate dehydrogenase, fumarase and aconitase
Citrate synthase, isocitrate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex
Citrate synthase, succinate thiokinase and malate dehydrogenase
PDH complex, pyruvate carboxylase and malic enzyme
questions.explanation: These three enzymes catalyse the irreversible, regulated steps of the cycle and respond to the energy state of the cell (ATP/ADP, NADH/NAD⁺, Ca²⁺). Aconitase, fumarase and malate DH catalyse near-equilibrium reactions.

questions.stem: Ca²⁺ released during muscle contraction stimulates which TCA-cycle enzymes?
options: Citrate synthase and malate dehydrogenase
Succinate dehydrogenase and fumarase
Aconitase and citrate synthase
Isocitrate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex
Malate dehydrogenase and succinate thiokinase
questions.explanation: As taught, Ca²⁺ activates isocitrate DH and α-KGDH, linking TCA flux to muscle activity. Citrate synthase is activated by ADP but is not listed as a Ca²⁺ target.

questions.stem: If succinyl CoA accumulates in the mitochondria, which TCA-cycle enzymes are directly inhibited by it, as taught?
options: Citrate synthase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex
Isocitrate dehydrogenase and malate dehydrogenase
Fumarase and aconitase
Succinate dehydrogenase and isocitrate dehydrogenase
Malate dehydrogenase and fumarase
questions.explanation: Succinyl CoA, the product of α-KGDH, inhibits the enzyme that makes it and the first enzyme of the cycle, citrate synthase. Isocitrate DH is inhibited by NADH and ATP but not by succinyl CoA.

questions.stem: What is the effect of a high mitochondrial NADH/NAD⁺ ratio on the TCA cycle?
options: It activates isocitrate dehydrogenase and α-KGDH, speeding the cycle
It has no effect, because NADH is not a TCA regulator
It inhibits citrate synthase, isocitrate dehydrogenase and α-KGDH, slowing the cycle
It activates citrate synthase only
It inhibits succinate dehydrogenase only
questions.explanation: NADH is a product of the cycle and inhibits all three regulated enzymes, so the cycle slows when the ETC cannot keep up with NADH re-oxidation. A low NADH/NAD⁺ ratio relieves this inhibition.

questions.stem: A rise in mitochondrial ADP (a low-energy state) affects the TCA cycle by:
options: Inhibiting citrate synthase and isocitrate dehydrogenase
Activating citrate synthase and isocitrate dehydrogenase
Inhibiting α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase only
Inhibiting all three regulated enzymes
Having no effect on the TCA cycle
questions.explanation: ADP signals a need for ATP and, as taught, activates citrate synthase and isocitrate dehydrogenase, increasing the supply of NADH and FADH₂ to the ETC. ATP has the opposite, inhibitory effect.

questions.stem: As taught, citrate synthase is inhibited by all of the following EXCEPT:
options: ATP
ADP
NADH
Succinyl CoA
Citrate
questions.explanation: Citrate synthase is inhibited by ATP, NADH, succinyl CoA and its own product citrate, but it is activated by ADP. ADP rises when energy is needed, so it speeds the cycle.

questions.stem: During a sprint, TCA-cycle flux in skeletal muscle rises sharply. Which combination of signals is mainly responsible?
options: ↑ ATP and ↑ NADH/NAD⁺ ratio
↑ Succinyl CoA and ↑ citrate
↓ Ca²⁺ and ↑ ATP/ADP ratio
↑ NADH and ↓ ADP
↑ Ca²⁺, ↑ ADP and ↓ NADH/NAD⁺ ratio
questions.explanation: Contraction releases Ca²⁺ (activating isocitrate DH and α-KGDH), consumes ATP (raising ADP, which activates citrate synthase and isocitrate DH), and the active ETC keeps NADH low. ATP, NADH, succinyl CoA and citrate are all inhibitory signals.

questions.stem: Why does accumulation of ATP in a resting, well-fed cell slow the TCA cycle?
options: ATP competitively inhibits succinate dehydrogenase at Complex II
ATP covalently phosphorylates and inactivates aconitase
ATP allosterically inhibits citrate synthase, isocitrate dehydrogenase and α-KGDH
ATP is consumed as a substrate in every turn of the cycle
ATP binds Ca²⁺ and thereby activates isocitrate dehydrogenase
questions.explanation: As taught, ATP inhibits all three regulated enzymes, so fuel oxidation is matched to energy need. The cycle does not consume ATP; it produces GTP.

questions.stem: The TCA cycle is described as amphibolic because it:
options: Operates in both the cytosol and the mitochondria
Functions both in catabolism (oxidizing fuels) and in anabolism (supplying biosynthetic precursors)
Works both aerobically and anaerobically
Uses NADP⁺ exclusively as its electron acceptor
Is freely reversible at every step
questions.explanation: The cycle oxidizes acetyl CoA to CO₂ (catabolic) while its intermediates are drawn off for glucose, lipid, amino acid and heme synthesis (anabolic). It is strictly mitochondrial and depends indirectly on O₂.
questions.origin: Adapted from OMC-tagged Studocu question bank (essay prompt converted to MCQ; unverified student upload)

questions.stem: Which anaplerotic reaction is the most important for replenishing oxaloacetate in the TCA cycle?
options: PDH complex: pyruvate → acetyl CoA + CO₂
Lactate dehydrogenase: pyruvate → lactate
Alanine transaminase: pyruvate → alanine
Citrate synthase: oxaloacetate + acetyl CoA → citrate
Pyruvate carboxylase: pyruvate + CO₂ + ATP → oxaloacetate
questions.explanation: Anaplerotic reactions refill cycle intermediates, and pyruvate carboxylase forms oxaloacetate directly. The PDH reaction supplies acetyl CoA, which is oxidized but cannot increase the amount of cycle intermediates.

questions.stem: In the lecture's amphibolic figure, which TCA intermediate is the direct exit point to gluconeogenesis?
options: Acetyl CoA
Citrate
Succinyl CoA
α-Ketoglutarate
Oxaloacetate
questions.explanation: Oxaloacetate is converted to phosphoenolpyruvate and then to glucose, linking the cycle with gluconeogenesis. Citrate exits for lipid synthesis, succinyl CoA for heme synthesis and α-ketoglutarate for glutamate.

questions.stem: Developing red cells in the bone marrow synthesize large amounts of heme. Which TCA intermediate do they withdraw for this purpose?
options: Citrate
α-Ketoglutarate
Oxaloacetate
Succinyl CoA
Fumarate
questions.explanation: Succinyl CoA condenses with glycine in the first step of heme synthesis, which is why it appears in the amphibolic figure as the link to heme. Citrate supplies acetyl CoA for lipids, while α-ketoglutarate and oxaloacetate supply glutamate and aspartate.

questions.stem: Citrate exported from the mitochondria to the cytosol serves mainly as a source of:
options: Oxaloacetate for heme synthesis
Succinyl CoA for ketone body synthesis
Acetyl CoA for fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis
Glutamate for protein synthesis
Pyruvate for glycolysis
questions.explanation: Acetyl CoA cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane, so it leaves as citrate, which is cleaved in the cytosol to release acetyl CoA for lipid synthesis. This is the citrate/acetyl CoA → lipid synthesis arm of the amphibolic figure.

questions.stem: Glutamate dehydrogenase links the TCA cycle with amino acid metabolism through which intermediate?
options: α-Ketoglutarate
Oxaloacetate
Succinyl CoA
Fumarate
Citrate
questions.explanation: Glutamate dehydrogenase interconverts α-ketoglutarate and glutamate, so the cycle can supply carbon skeletons for amino acid and protein synthesis. Oxaloacetate is linked to aspartate by AST.

questions.stem: Aspartate transaminase (AST) connects the TCA cycle to amino acid metabolism by interconverting:
options: Oxaloacetate and aspartate
Pyruvate and alanine
Succinyl CoA and glycine
Citrate and acetyl CoA
Fumarate and malate
questions.explanation: AST transfers an amino group to oxaloacetate to form aspartate (and back), providing aspartate for protein synthesis. Pyruvate ↔ alanine is the ALT reaction.

questions.stem: Propionyl CoA, derived from odd-chain fatty acids and some amino acids, enters the TCA cycle as:
options: Succinyl CoA
Acetyl CoA
α-Ketoglutarate
Oxaloacetate
Citrate
questions.explanation: Propionyl CoA is converted (via methylmalonyl CoA) to succinyl CoA, shown in the lecture figure as propionyl CoA ↔ succinyl CoA. Because it adds a cycle intermediate, this route is anaplerotic.

questions.stem: Why can acetyl CoA from fatty acid oxidation NOT provide net synthesis of oxaloacetate for gluconeogenesis?
options: Acetyl CoA cannot enter the mitochondrial matrix
Citrate synthase is absent from the liver
The two carbons it brings in are lost as two CO₂ in the same turn, so there is no net gain of oxaloacetate
Acetyl CoA is converted directly to glucose by malic enzyme
Acetyl CoA irreversibly inhibits the TCA cycle
questions.explanation: For every acetyl CoA that enters, one oxaloacetate is used and one is regenerated while two CO₂ leave, so the pool of intermediates does not grow. Net gluconeogenesis requires anaplerotic input such as pyruvate carboxylase.

questions.stem: Oxidative phosphorylation is best defined as:
options: The coupling of electron transport from NADH and FADH₂ to O₂ with the synthesis of ATP from ADP + Pi
Formation of ATP from a high-energy substrate without the ETC or molecular O₂
Transfer of phosphate from ATP to glucose
Oxidation of fatty acids in peroxisomes
Hydrolysis of ATP to pump protons out of the matrix
questions.explanation: In oxidative phosphorylation, energy released as electrons flow to O₂ is captured as a proton gradient and used to phosphorylate ADP. ATP formation without the ETC or O₂ is substrate-level phosphorylation.

questions.stem: Substrate-level phosphorylation differs from oxidative phosphorylation because it:
options: Requires a proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane
Forms ATP (or GTP) directly from a high-energy substrate, without the ETC or molecular O₂
Requires the activity of cytochrome c oxidase
Occurs only on the inner mitochondrial membrane
Produces most of the ATP of aerobic cells
questions.explanation: Substrate-level phosphorylation transfers phosphate directly from an energy-rich substrate, as in glycolysis and at succinate thiokinase in the TCA cycle. Most ATP in aerobic cells comes from oxidative phosphorylation, which needs the ETC, O₂ and the proton gradient.
questions.origin: Adapted from OMC-tagged Studocu question bank (essay prompt converted to MCQ; unverified student upload)

questions.stem: In the reaction NADH → NAD⁺ + H⁺ + 2e⁻, NADH is:
options: Reduced, because it loses electrons
Reduced, because it releases a proton
Phosphorylated, because it forms NAD⁺
Oxidized, because it loses electrons
Neither oxidized nor reduced, because only H⁺ is released
questions.explanation: Oxidation is loss of electrons and reduction is gain of electrons. NADH donates its electrons to Complex I and is thereby oxidized to NAD⁺.

questions.stem: Complex I of the electron transport chain is:
options: Succinate dehydrogenase, containing FAD and Fe–S centres
The cytochrome bc1 complex, containing cytochromes b and c1
Cytochrome c oxidase, containing cytochromes a, a₃ and copper
NADH dehydrogenase, containing FMN and iron–sulfur (Fe–S) centres
ATP synthase, containing Fo and F1 domains
questions.explanation: Complex I accepts electrons from NADH via FMN and passes them through Fe–S centres to coenzyme Q. The other options describe Complexes II, III, IV and V respectively.

questions.stem: Which ETC complex contains cytochromes a and a₃ together with two copper centres (CuA and CuB)?
options: Complex I
Complex II
Complex III
Complex IV
Complex V (ATP synthase)
questions.explanation: Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) transfers electrons from cytochrome c to O₂ using cytochromes a/a₃ and CuA/CuB. Complex III contains cytochromes b and c1 but no copper.
questions.origin: Adapted from OMC-tagged Studocu question bank (essay prompt converted to MCQ; unverified student upload)

questions.stem: Which two components act as mobile electron carriers in the electron transport chain?
options: FMN and FAD
Cytochrome b and cytochrome c1
CuA and CuB
Fe–S proteins and cytochrome a₃
Coenzyme Q (ubiquinone) and cytochrome c
questions.explanation: Lipid-soluble coenzyme Q shuttles electrons within the membrane from Complexes I and II to Complex III, and cytochrome c carries them from Complex III to Complex IV. The other pairs are fixed prosthetic groups inside individual complexes.

questions.stem: An infant has an inherited deficiency of Complex I. Electrons from which source can still reach coenzyme Q normally?
options: NADH from malate dehydrogenase
NADH from isocitrate dehydrogenase
FADH₂ from succinate dehydrogenase (Complex II)
NADH from the PDH complex
NADH from the α-KGDH complex
questions.explanation: All NADH must be oxidized by Complex I, whereas FADH₂ from succinate dehydrogenase (Complex II) passes its electrons directly to coenzyme Q, bypassing Complex I. Because Complex I is bypassed, oxidation of each FADH₂ drives the pumping of fewer protons (6) than each NADH (10).

questions.stem: Cytochrome c is a small, water-soluble protein loosely attached to the outer face of the inner mitochondrial membrane. If it is lost from the mitochondria, electron flow is interrupted between:
options: Complex I and coenzyme Q
Complex II and coenzyme Q
Coenzyme Q and Complex III
Complex IV and O₂
Complex III and Complex IV
questions.explanation: Electrons from NADH flow NADH → Complex I → CoQ → Complex III → cytochrome c → Complex IV → O₂, so cytochrome c is the link between Complexes III and IV. Coenzyme Q, not cytochrome c, links Complexes I and II to Complex III.

questions.stem: How do cytochromes carry electrons in the ETC?
options: By binding and releasing ATP
By accepting two hydrogen atoms at a time, as coenzyme Q does
By covalently accepting acetyl groups
By reversible Fe³⁺ ⇌ Fe²⁺ changes of the iron in their heme group
By reversible oxidation of a copper ion only
questions.explanation: Each cytochrome contains a heme whose iron is alternately reduced (Fe²⁺) and oxidized (Fe³⁺) as it accepts and donates single electrons. Copper centres occur only in Complex IV, alongside cytochromes a and a₃.
questions.origin: Adapted from OMC-tagged Studocu question bank (essay prompt converted to MCQ; unverified student upload)

questions.stem: Complex III of the electron transport chain is also known as:
options: Cytochrome c oxidase
The cytochrome bc1 complex (cytochromes b, c1 and Fe–S)
NADH dehydrogenase
Succinate dehydrogenase
F1Fo-ATPase
questions.explanation: Complex III accepts electrons from reduced coenzyme Q and passes them to cytochrome c using cytochromes b and c1 and an Fe–S centre. Cytochrome c oxidase is Complex IV.

questions.stem: Which outline of aerobic cellular respiration matches the locations taught in the lecture?
options: Glycolysis in the matrix → TCA cycle in the cytosol → ETC in the outer membrane
Glycolysis in the cytosol → pyruvate enters mitochondria → acetyl CoA and TCA cycle in the matrix → NADH/FADH₂ oxidized by the ETC in the inner membrane
Glycolysis in the cytosol → TCA cycle in the intermembrane space → ETC in the outer membrane
Glycolysis in the cytosol → TCA cycle in the cytosol → ETC in the inner membrane
Glycolysis in the inner membrane → TCA cycle in the matrix → ETC in the cytosol
questions.explanation: Glycolysis is cytosolic; pyruvate is carried into the matrix for PDH and the TCA cycle; and the ETC complexes sit in the inner mitochondrial membrane (cristae), where ½O₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂O.

questions.stem: A child with a rare mitochondrial disorder cannot synthesize adequate coenzyme Q (ubiquinone). Which electron transfers would be impaired?
options: Transfer from both Complex I (NADH) and Complex II (FADH₂) to Complex III
Only transfer from Complex III to Complex IV
Only transfer from Complex IV to O₂
Only transfer from NADH to Complex I
None, because cytochrome c can replace coenzyme Q
questions.explanation: Coenzyme Q collects electrons from both Complex I and Complex II and delivers them to Complex III, so its deficiency impairs oxidation of both NADH and FADH₂. Cytochrome c works downstream, between Complexes III and IV, and cannot substitute.

questions.stem: According to Peter Mitchell's chemiosmotic theory, the energy released by electron transport is first conserved as:
options: A proton gradient (proton motive force) across the inner mitochondrial membrane
A high-energy phosphorylated intermediate of Complex I
GTP formed in the mitochondrial matrix
A conformational change stored in cytochrome c
Heat released into the matrix
questions.explanation: Complexes I, III and IV pump H⁺ into the intermembrane space, creating a pH and electrical gradient; H⁺ flowing back through ATP synthase drives ATP synthesis. Heat is the outcome only when the gradient is dissipated, as with uncouplers.
questions.origin: Adapted from OMC-tagged Studocu question bank (essay prompt converted to MCQ; unverified student upload)

questions.stem: Which complexes pump protons, and how many per pair of electrons, as taught?
options: Complex I: 4 H⁺; Complex II: 4 H⁺; Complex IV: 2 H⁺
Complex I: 2 H⁺; Complex III: 2 H⁺; Complex IV: 2 H⁺
Complex I: 4 H⁺; Complex III: 2 H⁺; Complex IV: 4 H⁺
Complex I: 4 H⁺; Complex III: 4 H⁺; Complex IV: 2 H⁺
Complex II: 4 H⁺; Complex III: 4 H⁺; Complex IV: 2 H⁺
questions.explanation: Complexes I, III and IV pump 4, 4 and 2 protons respectively, giving 10 H⁺ per NADH. Complex II does not pump protons.

questions.stem: Mitochondria are given succinate as their only substrate, with rotenone present to block Complex I. Which complexes pump protons under these conditions?
options: Complexes I, III and IV
Complexes II, III and IV
Complexes III and IV only
Complex II only
Complex IV only
questions.explanation: Succinate's electrons enter at Complex II, which does not pump protons, and then pass through Complexes III and IV, which pump 4 + 2 = 6 H⁺. Complex I is both bypassed and blocked.

questions.stem: During active electron transport, how does the intermembrane space compare with the matrix?
options: It is more alkaline and positively charged
It is more acidic and negatively charged
It is more acidic (lower pH) and positively charged
It has the same pH; only an electrical gradient exists
It is more alkaline and negatively charged
questions.explanation: Pumped protons accumulate in the intermembrane space, lowering its pH and making it positive relative to the matrix, which becomes alkaline and negative. Together, the chemical and electrical components form the proton motive force.

questions.stem: How many protons are pumped into the intermembrane space when one NADH is oxidized by the ETC, as taught?
questions.explanation: Complex I (4) + Complex III (4) + Complex IV (2) = 10 H⁺ per NADH. FADH₂, entering at Complex II, gives only 6.

questions.stem: Why does oxidation of FADH₂ yield fewer ATP than oxidation of NADH?
options: FADH₂ carries only one electron instead of two
Its electrons enter at Complex II and bypass Complex I, so only 6 H⁺ are pumped instead of 10
Its electrons enter at Complex IV and bypass Complex III
Its electrons are not transferred to O₂
Complex II consumes ATP to accept electrons from FADH₂
questions.explanation: Electrons from FADH₂ reach coenzyme Q via Complex II, which does not pump protons, so only Complexes III and IV pump (4 + 2 = 6 H⁺), giving about 1.5 ATP instead of 2.5. FADH₂ still donates two electrons that end up on O₂.

questions.stem: If 4 H⁺ must flow back through ATP synthase to make one ATP, how many ATP are produced from the 6 H⁺ pumped when one FADH₂ is oxidized?
options: 1 ATP
1.5 ATP
2 ATP
2.5 ATP
3 ATP
questions.explanation: 6 H⁺ ÷ 4 H⁺ per ATP = 1.5 ATP. By the same reasoning NADH gives 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5 ATP.

questions.stem: Why must the inner mitochondrial membrane be impermeable to H⁺ for oxidative phosphorylation to work?
options: Protons are substrates consumed by Complex II
Protons must re-enter the matrix only through ATP synthase, so that the gradient drives ATP formation
Free leakage of H⁺ would increase ATP synthesis
ATP synthase is located in the outer membrane
The outer membrane, not the inner membrane, maintains the gradient
questions.explanation: If protons could leak back freely, the proton motive force would dissipate without passing through ATP synthase, which is exactly how uncouplers abolish ATP synthesis. The gradient is across the inner membrane; the outer membrane is freely permeable to small ions.

questions.stem: The slides mention an OLDER Lippincott convention for ATP yield. What values did it assign per NADH and per FADH₂?
options: 3 ATP per NADH and 2 ATP per FADH₂
2.5 ATP per NADH and 1.5 ATP per FADH₂
2 ATP per NADH and 1 ATP per FADH₂
4 ATP per NADH and 3 ATP per FADH₂
10 ATP per NADH and 6 ATP per FADH₂
questions.explanation: The older convention used 3 and 2 ATP; the current convention used in this course (4 H⁺ per ATP) gives 2.5 and 1.5. The values 10 and 6 are the numbers of protons pumped, not ATP.

questions.stem: In intact, coupled mitochondria, the rate of electron transport and O₂ consumption is mainly controlled by:
options: The concentration of CO₂ in the matrix
The amount of glucose in the cytosol
The availability of ADP (and Pi) for ATP synthase
The rate of cytochrome c synthesis
The permeability of the outer mitochondrial membrane
questions.explanation: Because electron transport and phosphorylation are tightly coupled, the ETC runs only as fast as protons can re-enter through ATP synthase, which needs ADP + Pi (respiratory control). Uncouplers remove this control, so O₂ consumption rises even without ADP.

questions.stem: Which description of ATP synthase (Complex V) is correct?
options: Fo spans the inner membrane and forms the H⁺ channel (c-ring); F1 projects into the matrix and carries the catalytic activity
F1 spans the inner membrane and forms the H⁺ channel; Fo projects into the matrix and carries the catalytic activity
It is a single polypeptide located in the outer mitochondrial membrane
It contains cytochromes a and a₃ with copper centres
It contains FMN and iron–sulfur centres
questions.explanation: ATP synthase has a membrane Fo domain (proton channel with c-rings) and an extra-membranous F1 domain in the matrix (α, β, γ, δ, ε subunits) that makes ATP. Cytochromes with copper describe Complex IV, and FMN with Fe–S describes Complex I.

questions.stem: The catalytic (ATP-synthesizing) activity of ATP synthase resides in:
options: The Fo c-ring within the membrane
The intermembrane-space side of Fo
Cytochrome c bound to the complex
The F1 domain facing the matrix
The outer mitochondrial membrane
questions.explanation: F1, the extra-membranous matrix domain, contains the catalytic activity that joins ADP and Pi. Fo is the proton channel that powers it.

questions.stem: Which subunits make up the F1 domain of ATP synthase, as taught?
options: E1, E2 and E3
Cytochromes b and c1 with an Fe–S protein
Cytochromes a and a₃ with CuA and CuB
α, β, γ, δ and ε
FMN and Fe–S proteins
questions.explanation: F1 is a multisubunit head (α, β, γ, δ, ε) projecting into the matrix. E1–E3 are the enzymes of the PDH-type complexes, and the cytochrome sets belong to Complexes III and IV.

questions.stem: What directly drives ATP synthesis by ATP synthase?
options: Flow of H⁺ from the matrix out to the intermembrane space through Fo
Direct transfer of electrons from cytochrome c to F1
Hydrolysis of GTP produced by the TCA cycle
Influx of Na⁺ ions into the matrix
Flow of H⁺ from the intermembrane space back into the matrix through Fo
questions.explanation: Protons move down their electrochemical gradient, from the acidic intermembrane space into the matrix, through the Fo channel, and F1 uses this energy to make ATP. Pumping H⁺ out of the matrix is the job of Complexes I, III and IV.

questions.stem: How is the energy of proton flow through Fo converted into ATP?
options: Protons are incorporated directly into the ATP molecule
Electrons flowing through F1 reduce ADP to ATP
Proton flow rotates the Fo c-ring, and the rotation transmitted to F1 causes conformational changes that join ADP and Pi
Cytochrome c binds F1 and donates a phosphate group
F1 pumps protons out of the matrix, releasing ATP
questions.explanation: ATP synthase is a rotary machine: H⁺ entering through the c-ring makes it turn, and the rotating central stalk changes the shape of the catalytic sites in F1 so that ATP is formed and released. No electrons pass through ATP synthase.

questions.stem: In the numbering of the oxidative phosphorylation system, ATP synthase (F1Fo-ATPase) is referred to as:
options: Complex I
Complex II
Complex III
Complex IV
Complex V
questions.explanation: ATP synthase is often called Complex V, although it does not transfer electrons; it uses the proton gradient produced by Complexes I, III and IV. Complex IV is cytochrome c oxidase.

questions.stem: A gardener accidentally ingests a rotenone-based pesticide. Rotenone belongs to the same inhibitor group (acting at the same ETC site) as:
options: Antimycin A and dimercaprol
Cyanide and hydrogen sulfide
Oligomycin
2,4-Dinitrophenol and salicylate
Amobarbital and piericidin
questions.explanation: Rotenone, amobarbital and piericidin all inhibit Complex I, blocking electron transfer from NADH to coenzyme Q. Antimycin A and BAL act at Complex III, cyanide and H₂S at Complex IV, oligomycin on ATP synthase, and DNP and salicylate are uncouplers.

questions.stem: Antimycin A blocks electron flow at:
options: Complex I
Complex II
Complex III
Complex IV
ATP synthase (Fo)
questions.explanation: Antimycin A inhibits Complex III (cytochrome bc1), as does dimercaprol (BAL) as taught. Oligomycin is the agent that acts on the Fo domain of ATP synthase.

questions.stem: A firefighter rescued from a burning building full of smouldering plastics has severe lactic acidosis, and his venous blood is unusually bright red with an abnormally high O₂ content. Which ETC component is most likely inhibited?
options: Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase)
Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase)
Complex III (cytochrome bc1)
Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase)
ATP synthase (Fo domain)
questions.explanation: Smoke from burning plastics contains cyanide (and CO), which bind Complex IV and stop electron transfer to O₂; tissues cannot use O₂, so venous blood stays oxygenated and ATP must come from glycolysis, producing lactate. Complex I and III inhibitors such as rotenone and antimycin A are not smoke toxins.

questions.stem: A sewer worker collapses within minutes of exposure to a gas that smells of rotten eggs. This gas inhibits the same ETC component as:
options: Rotenone
Antimycin A
Oligomycin
2,4-Dinitrophenol
Cyanide
questions.explanation: Hydrogen sulfide (H₂S), like cyanide and CO, inhibits Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase). Rotenone acts on Complex I, antimycin A on Complex III, oligomycin on ATP synthase, and DNP is an uncoupler.

questions.stem: Dimercaprol (British anti-Lewisite, BAL), as classified in this course, inhibits:
options: Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase)
Complex III (cytochrome bc1 complex)
Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase)
The Fo domain of ATP synthase
Nothing in the ETC; it acts as an uncoupler
questions.explanation: In the lecture's classification, BAL is listed with antimycin A as a Complex III inhibitor. Rotenone and amobarbital act at Complex I, and cyanide, CO and H₂S at Complex IV.

questions.stem: Oligomycin inhibits oxidative phosphorylation by:
options: Binding cytochrome a₃ of Complex IV
Making the inner membrane permeable to H⁺
Blocking electron transfer from Complex I to coenzyme Q
Inhibiting cytochrome b of Complex III
Binding the Fo domain of ATP synthase and blocking H⁺ re-entry into the matrix
questions.explanation: Oligomycin closes the proton channel of Fo, so phosphorylation stops; electron transport then also slows because the proton gradient cannot be discharged. Making the membrane leaky to H⁺ is the action of uncouplers.

questions.stem: Isolated mitochondria oxidizing malate (an NADH-generating substrate) are treated with rotenone, and O₂ consumption stops. Which addition would restore O₂ consumption and some ATP synthesis?
options: More malate
Succinate
Oligomycin
Cyanide
Antimycin A
questions.explanation: Rotenone blocks Complex I, but succinate donates electrons via Complex II (FADH₂) to coenzyme Q, bypassing the block, so about 1.5 ATP per FADH₂ can still be made. Antimycin A and cyanide block downstream of coenzyme Q, and oligomycin blocks ATP synthase.

questions.stem: Mitochondria are treated with oligomycin, and both ATP synthesis and O₂ consumption fall. 2,4-Dinitrophenol (DNP) is then added. What happens?
options: Both O₂ consumption and ATP synthesis resume
Neither O₂ consumption nor ATP synthesis changes
ATP synthesis resumes, but O₂ consumption stays inhibited
O₂ consumption falls to zero and ATP synthesis increases
O₂ consumption resumes, but ATP synthesis remains inhibited
questions.explanation: With ATP synthase blocked, the gradient builds up and slows electron transport; DNP lets protons leak back across the membrane, so electron transport and O₂ use restart. ATP synthase is still blocked by oligomycin, so no ATP is made and the energy is lost as heat.

questions.stem: In mitochondria treated with antimycin A, which carriers become fully reduced?
options: NADH, the Complex I centres and coenzyme Q, which lie upstream of Complex III
Cytochrome c and Complex IV, which lie downstream of Complex III
None; all carriers become fully oxidized
Only cytochrome a₃
Only the F1 domain of ATP synthase
questions.explanation: Carriers before a block cannot pass on their electrons and stay reduced, while carriers after the block give up their electrons to O₂ and become oxidized. Antimycin A blocks Complex III, so coenzyme Q and everything upstream are reduced.

questions.stem: A patient takes an overdose of amobarbital, a barbiturate. At the mitochondrial level, which step of electron transport does this drug directly block?
options: Transfer of electrons from cytochrome c to O₂ at Complex IV
Transfer of electrons from Complex I to coenzyme Q
Transfer of electrons from coenzyme Q to cytochrome c at Complex III
Transfer of electrons from FADH₂ at Complex II
Re-entry of H⁺ through the Fo domain of ATP synthase
questions.explanation: Amobarbital, like rotenone and piericidin, is a Complex I inhibitor, so NADH-linked oxidation stops while succinate (FADH₂) can still be oxidized via Complex II. Cyanide acts at Complex IV and oligomycin at Fo.

questions.stem: Uncouplers of oxidative phosphorylation act by:
options: Making the inner mitochondrial membrane permeable to H⁺, so electron transport continues without ATP synthesis
Blocking electron transfer at Complex IV
Binding the Fo domain and preventing H⁺ re-entry
Inhibiting the PDH complex
Blocking electron transfer from Complex I to coenzyme Q
questions.explanation: Uncouplers let protons leak back into the matrix without passing through ATP synthase, abolishing the proton motive force; electron flow continues but the energy is lost as heat. Blocking Fo is oligomycin's action.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an uncoupler of oxidative phosphorylation?
options: Rotenone
Antimycin A
2,4-Dinitrophenol
Oligomycin
Cyanide
questions.explanation: 2,4-DNP is a lipid-soluble weak acid that carries protons across the inner membrane, dissipating the gradient. The others are site-specific inhibitors: rotenone (Complex I), antimycin A (III), cyanide (IV) and oligomycin (ATP synthase).

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an uncoupler?
options: 2,4-Dinitrophenol
Oligomycin
Dicumarol
Salicylate (high dose)
Thermogenin (UCP1)
questions.explanation: Oligomycin inhibits ATP synthase by blocking Fo, so it stops ATP synthesis and, secondarily, electron transport. DNP, dicumarol, high-dose salicylate and the uncoupling protein thermogenin all dissipate the proton gradient.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man taking an illicit 'fat-burner' containing 2,4-dinitrophenol presents with hyperthermia, profuse sweating and tachycardia. Which set of mitochondrial changes is expected?
options: ↓ O₂ consumption, ↓ ATP synthesis, ↓ heat production
↑ O₂ consumption, ↓ ATP synthesis, ↑ heat production
↑ O₂ consumption, ↑ ATP synthesis, ↓ heat production
↓ O₂ consumption, ↑ ATP synthesis, ↑ heat production
No change in O₂ consumption, ↑ ATP synthesis, no change in heat
questions.explanation: DNP uncouples: electron transport speeds up (more O₂ used) as the cell tries to restore the gradient, but protons bypass ATP synthase, so ATP falls and the energy is released as heat, causing hyperthermia. Decreased O₂ consumption would point to an ETC inhibitor instead.

questions.stem: A newborn in a cool delivery room maintains body temperature without shivering. Which protein is mainly responsible?
options: Cytochrome c oxidase in skeletal muscle
ATP synthase in white adipose tissue
Thermogenin (UCP1) in brown adipose tissue
Haemoglobin in erythrocytes
Myosin ATPase in skeletal muscle
questions.explanation: Thermogenin is a physiological uncoupler: it forms a proton channel in the inner membrane of brown fat mitochondria, so the energy of electron transport is released as heat (non-shivering thermogenesis) instead of being used for ATP synthesis.
questions.origin: Adapted from OMC-tagged Studocu question bank (essay prompt converted to MCQ; unverified student upload)

questions.stem: A child who ingested a large quantity of aspirin develops fever and rapid breathing. Which mechanism best explains the fever?
options: Salicylate inhibits Complex IV in the same way as cyanide
High-dose salicylate uncouples oxidative phosphorylation, so energy is released as heat
Salicylate increases ATP synthesis by ATP synthase
Salicylate blocks the Fo domain in the same way as oligomycin
Salicylate stimulates thermogenin production in white adipose tissue
questions.explanation: At high doses salicylate acts as an uncoupler, making the inner membrane leaky to H⁺; electron transport and O₂ use increase while ATP falls, and the energy appears as heat. It is not a site-specific ETC or ATP synthase inhibitor.

questions.stem: In the presence of an uncoupler, the energy released by electron transport is mainly:
options: Released as heat
Stored as ATP
Stored as GTP
Stored as NADPH
Stored as a larger proton gradient
questions.explanation: Because the proton gradient collapses, no proton motive force is available for ATP synthase, and the free energy of electron transport is dissipated as heat (thermogenesis).

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes an uncoupler such as DNP from an ETC inhibitor such as cyanide?
options: Both increase O₂ consumption
Both stop electron flow completely
An uncoupler increases O₂ consumption while abolishing ATP synthesis; cyanide stops both O₂ consumption and ATP synthesis
An uncoupler stops O₂ consumption, whereas cyanide increases it
An uncoupler increases ATP synthesis, whereas cyanide decreases it
questions.explanation: Uncouplers leave the ETC running, often faster, but disconnect it from ATP synthesis; site-specific inhibitors physically block electron flow, so O₂ is no longer reduced and no gradient forms.

questions.stem: As taught, by which mechanism does glucose cross the brush-border (apical) membrane from the intestinal lumen into the enterocyte?
options: Simple diffusion through the lipid bilayer, down the concentration gradient
Facilitated diffusion through GLUT-2 (uniport), without Na⁺
Secondary active transport through SGLT-1, in symport with Na⁺
Primary active transport by a glucose-specific ATPase pump
Insulin-stimulated facilitated diffusion through GLUT-4
questions.explanation: SGLT-1 on the brush border moves glucose into the enterocyte against its gradient together with Na⁺; the energy comes from Na⁺ moving down the gradient that the basolateral Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase maintains, so ATP is used only indirectly (secondary active transport). GLUT-2 is the basolateral exit route, and enterocytes do not rely on GLUT-4.

questions.stem: After absorption, glucose leaves the enterocyte across the basolateral membrane to enter the portal blood through:
options: GLUT-2, by facilitated diffusion (uniport)
SGLT-1, by Na⁺ cotransport
GLUT-4, after insulin-stimulated translocation
The Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase
SGLT-2, by Na⁺ cotransport
questions.explanation: Glucose concentrated inside the enterocyte by SGLT-1 leaves down its concentration gradient through the GLUT-2 uniporter. The Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase on the same membrane pumps ions, not glucose, and SGLT-2 is the renal proximal-tubule transporter.

questions.stem: In an isolated strip of small-intestinal epithelium, ouabain is added to block the basolateral Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase. Glucose uptake from the lumen soon falls sharply, although SGLT-1 itself is not inhibited. Why?
options: Ouabain binds GLUT-2 on the basolateral membrane and traps glucose inside the cell
The Na⁺ gradient that drives SGLT-1 collapses, so glucose can no longer be taken up against its gradient
Intracellular ATP rises because the pump no longer consumes it, and the excess ATP allosterically inhibits SGLT-1
Hexokinase is inhibited, so glucose is no longer trapped inside the enterocyte
GLUT-4 vesicles can no longer fuse with the brush-border membrane
questions.explanation: SGLT-1 is secondary active transport: it uses the energy of Na⁺ flowing into the cell, and that low intracellular Na⁺ is maintained by the basolateral Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase. When the pump is blocked, intracellular Na⁺ rises, the gradient collapses and Na⁺-coupled glucose uptake fails; GLUT-4 is not the intestinal transporter.

questions.stem: Which glucose transporter is insulin-dependent and is found mainly in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue?
options: GLUT-1
GLUT-2
GLUT-3
GLUT-4
SGLT-1
questions.explanation: Insulin causes GLUT-4 to move from intracellular vesicles to the plasma membrane of skeletal muscle and adipocytes, increasing glucose uptake after a meal. GLUT-1 (basal uptake in almost all tissues), GLUT-2 (liver and pancreas) and GLUT-3 (neurons) are not insulin-dependent.

questions.stem: Hepatocytes and pancreatic β-cells must take up glucose in proportion to its blood concentration so that they can 'sense' hyperglycaemia after a meal. Which transporter, and which property as taught, makes this possible?
options: GLUT-3, because its very low Km lets neurons take up glucose even when blood glucose is low after an overnight fast
GLUT-4, because insulin recruits it to the plasma membrane
SGLT-1, because it concentrates glucose against its gradient
GLUT-1, because it provides basal uptake in almost all tissues
GLUT-2, because its high Km means its transport rate keeps rising as blood glucose rises
questions.explanation: GLUT-2 has the highest Km of the GLUTs, so it is far from saturated at normal blood glucose and its transport rate rises with glycaemia, letting the liver and β-cells sense high glucose (together with high-Km glucokinase). A low-Km transporter such as GLUT-3 is already near saturation and cannot report changes in blood glucose.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man treated with insulin has a capillary blood glucose of 2.8 mmol/L. At such low concentrations, neurons continue to take up glucose relatively efficiently, whereas hepatic glucose uptake falls considerably. Which transporter on the neurons is mainly responsible for this?
options: GLUT-2
GLUT-3
GLUT-4
SGLT-1
SGLT-2
questions.explanation: Neuronal GLUT-3 has a low Km (the lowest of the GLUTs, as taught), so it stays close to saturation and keeps supplying the brain even when blood glucose is low. High-Km GLUT-2 in the liver slows as glucose falls, and GLUT-4 depends on insulin and is a muscle/adipose transporter.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes is started on dapagliflozin. Two weeks later her plasma glucose has fallen, and her urine dipstick shows marked glucosuria. Which transporter does this drug inhibit, and where?
options: GLUT-2 in the basolateral membrane of hepatocytes
SGLT-1 in the brush border of the small intestine
GLUT-4 in skeletal muscle
SGLT-2 in the proximal renal tubule
GLUT-1 in erythrocytes
questions.explanation: SGLT-2 reabsorbs filtered glucose in the proximal renal tubule by Na⁺-coupled secondary active transport; 'gliflozins' block it, so glucose is lost in the urine and plasma glucose falls. SGLT-1 is the intestinal isoform, and GLUT transporters are not Na⁺-coupled.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts GLUT transporters with SGLT transporters?
options: GLUTs carry glucose down its gradient by facilitated diffusion, in either direction; SGLTs carry it against its gradient, driven by Na⁺ entry
GLUTs hydrolyse ATP to pump glucose against its gradient; SGLTs let glucose diffuse passively down its gradient
GLUTs are found only in the intestine and kidney; SGLTs provide basal glucose uptake in almost all tissues
GLUTs cotransport Na⁺ together with glucose; SGLTs are uniporters that carry glucose alone
Both are insulin-dependent transporters that are stored in intracellular vesicles and recruited to the plasma membrane after a carbohydrate meal
questions.explanation: GLUTs are bidirectional facilitated-diffusion uniporters whose classes differ in affinity (Km); SGLTs are Na⁺–glucose symporters that use the Na⁺ gradient to move glucose uphill (SGLT1 in the small intestine, SGLT2 in the proximal renal tubule). Only GLUT-4 is insulin-dependent.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the overall purpose of glycolysis?
options: Oxidation of acetyl CoA to CO₂ and H₂O in the mitochondria, yielding NADH and FADH₂
Synthesis of glucose from pyruvate and lactate during fasting
Breakdown of one glucose (6C) into two pyruvate (3C), yielding ATP and NADH
Breakdown of liver glycogen to glucose 1-phosphate during fasting
Conversion of glucose 6-phosphate to ribose 5-phosphate and NADPH
questions.explanation: Glycolysis is the oxidative breakdown of glucose into two pyruvate, yielding ATP and NADH; aerobic glycolysis is the first stage of aerobic cellular respiration. The other options describe the TCA cycle, gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis and the pentose phosphate pathway.

questions.stem: Where does glycolysis take place?
